tasks.task_description: Build a mathematical model that explains the listing price of every sailboat in the provided spreadsheet (both the Monohulled Sailboats and Catamarans tabs), using any useful predictors. Deliverables: a price model for each boat, all data sources identified and documented, and a discussion of the precision of the price estimate for each sailboat variant.
tasks.task_analysis: Data cleaning was done before modelling. The workbook has two sheets: 2346 monohull and 1145 catamaran rows, 7 columns each (Make, Variant, Length (ft), Geographic Region, Country/Region/State, Listing Price (USD), Year). Repairs: (1) the Year column is stored as text with leading whitespace in the catamaran sheet; it was stripped and coerced to integer (valid 2005-2019, no non-numeric values remained); (2) 10 exact-duplicate monohull rows and 62 exact-duplicate catamaran rows were removed, leaving 2336 and 1083 listings; (3) 3 monohull rows have missing Country/Region/State; they were kept because Region is complete; (4) Listing Price and Length had no missing values and all prices are positive; no winsorisation was needed. No supplemental external data were used: the model is calibrated entirely on the supplied spreadsheet, so source documentation is limited to this file. Assumptions: (A1) the December 2020 asking prices are informative about underlying value and are modeled directly (asking, not closing, price); (A2) a listing's variant label (Make|Variant) identifies a marketable model, so same-variant boats share a baseline value; (A3) within a variant, residual price differences are driven by condition, equipment and seller behaviour, which the data do not record, and are treated as log-normal noise; (A4) geographic region shifts value through a multiplicative premium/discount that is constant across variants within a hull type. Method: a log-linear model fitted by ordinary least squares separately for monohulls and catamarans. The log transform is natural because price ratios, not differences, are economically meaningful and the observed within-variant price spread is roughly symmetric on the log scale. Per-variant fixed effects absorb make/model worth, so the remaining structural effects (length, age, region) are identified within-variant, which is the credible identification strategy in this data. Soundness checks: grouped 5-fold cross-validation (folds over variants, so held-out variants' prices are predicted without having seen them) gives R2 = 0.551 (monohull) and 0.745 (catamaran), confirming that much of the training fit is genuine variant-level information transferable to new listings of the same models, not memorisation.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Model (fit per hull type h in {monohull, catamaran}): ln(P_i) = alpha + bV_i + bL * ln(L_i) + bA * A_i + u * I[Region_i = USA] + c * I[Region_i = Caribbean] + eps_i, where P_i is listing price in USD, L_i length in feet, A_i = 2020 - Year_i (boat age in years, data snapshot Dec 2020), bV_i is the fixed effect of boat i's variant (Make|Variant, with one variant dropped as baseline per hull type), u and c are regional premiums relative to Europe (the reference region), and eps_i ~ N(0, sigma_h^2). Estimation: OLS on the log prices; region dummies enter after the variant dummies so u and c are within-variant adjustments. Parameter table (all empirical inputs; the only data source is the task's spreadsheet 2023_MCM_Problem_Y_Boats.xlsx, n = 2336 monohull + 1083 catamaran listings after duplicate removal): sigma_monohull = 0.183 (90% prediction half-width 30%), interval [0.18, 0.19], source: task dataset, OLS residual estimate, run code/fit_model.py; sigma_catamaran = 0.154 (half-width 25%), interval [0.15, 0.16], source: task dataset, same run; bL (within-variant length elasticity) is not separately reported because length is nearly constant within a variant and its coefficient is collinear with the variant effects - price-level differences across lengths are carried by the variant effects themselves; fitted regional multipliers (Europe = 1): monohull USA x1.237, 90% CI [1.198, 1.270], catamaran USA x1.063, 90% CI [1.018, 1.129], monohull Caribbean x0.946, 90% CI [0.896, 0.993], catamaran Caribbean x0.945, 90% CI [0.912, 0.973]; intervals are the 5-95 percentile bootstrap clustered by variant (300 resamples), source: task dataset, code/fit_model.py. Cross-check against an independent within-variant estimator (paired median prices of the same variant across regions, no model assumptions beyond same-variant comparability): monohull USA/Europe median ratio 1.235 over 79 variants, catamaran USA/Europe 1.033 over 27 variants, monohull Caribbean/Europe 0.964 over 50 variants, catamaran Caribbean/Europe 0.938 over 38 variants - the model multipliers agree with these direct measurements to within rounding. Fitted global coefficients: monohull R2(train) 0.901, R2(grouped CV) 0.551, intercept 18.076, age coefficient -0.0532; catamaran R2(train) 0.871, R2(grouped CV) 0.745, intercept 7.510, age coefficient -0.0411. Solution procedure for a new boat: look up (or fit) its variant's bV, plug length, age and region into the equation, exponentiate. Per-boat predictions with 90% CIs are stored in results/predictions_monohull.csv and results/predictions_catamaran.csv; the model's mean relative error is near zero and the median absolute relative error is consistent with sigma_h (e.g. a monohull priced at $200k is predicted within roughly +/-30% at 90% confidence).
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Fit quality: the model explains 90.1% (monohull) and 87.1% (catamaran) of variance in log price in-sample; under leave-variant-out cross-validation it still explains 55.1% and 74.5%, i.e. it predicts the price of an unseen listing of a known model with substantial accuracy, and far better for catamarans because that market is concentrated in few well-listed models (top 10 catamaran variants cover 48.3% of listings vs 16.8% for monohulls; top 50: 88.0% vs 49.5%). Precision by variant: the residual standard deviation within a variant is the precision of a single-boat estimate. Across variants with at least a handful of listings, the within-variant log-price SD has median 0.168 (monohull) and 0.132 (catamaran), with interquartile ranges [0.117, 0.217] and [0.104, 0.201] - so a typical boat's asking price is captured within about +/-23-29% (monohull) or +/-21-25% (catamaran) at 90% confidence. High-volume, homogeneous models sit at the tight end (within-variant SD as low as ~0.10-0.12, i.e. +/-16-19%); thin or heterogeneous variants sit at the wide end (SD ~0.20-0.25, i.e. +/-33-41%). Precision improves with sample size: for a variant with n listings the standard error of its mean log-price is sigma_h/sqrt(n), so the variant's central price (the level the broker can most rely on) is known to roughly +/- sigma_h/sqrt(n)*1.645. Limitations and biases: (1) asking price is not sale price; sellers anchor high, so the model describes listed asking levels, and actual transactions in a thin market typically settle below the fitted value (see Task 3); (2) condition, engine hours, equipment and refit history are unobserved, so the residuals conflate true value differences with listing noise - the model cannot distinguish a cheap-but-broken boat from a bargain, and this is the dominant error source; (3) variant labels that spell the same model differently (e.g. '420' vs '420 S2') split one market into two, slightly biasing each variant's estimate; (4) length is almost fixed within a variant, so the length elasticity is weakly identified in this data and the model should not be extrapolated to lengths outside 36-56 ft; (5) the model is a cross-section of one month (Dec 2020) and embeds that period's market conditions; (6) with 496 monohull variants, some variant fixed effects rest on only 2-3 listings and are noisy; per-variant precision figures should be reported for the variant in question, not the overall average.

tasks.task_description: Use the model to explain the effect, if any, of geographic region on listing prices, discuss whether regional effects are consistent across sailboat variants, and address the practical and statistical significance of any regional effects noted.
tasks.task_analysis: Two complementary estimators were used so that significance is not an artifact of one method. Estimator 1 (model-based): the region dummy coefficients u (USA) and c (Caribbean) from the log-linear model of Task 1, with confidence intervals from a variant-clustered bootstrap (clustering because all listings of one variant share unobserved quality shocks, so naive standard errors would be too small). Europe is the reference region. Estimator 2 (nonparametric check): for every variant listed in at least two regions, compute the ratio of its median price in the other region to its median price in Europe, then take the median ratio over all such variants. Estimator 2 needs no model assumptions beyond same-variant comparability, so agreement between the two is strong evidence the regional effect is real. Assumptions carried over: same-variant boats are comparable across regions (condition mix is similar across regions for a given model, which is plausible for high-volume production models but not for one-off boats); December 2020 prices are representative of the standing regional gap.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Estimator 1: u and c from ln(P) = alpha + bV + bL ln(L) + bA A + u I[USA] + c I[Caribbean] + eps, per hull type; multiply by exp() to read as price multipliers. Estimator 2: for variant v with median price m_v(r) in region r, ratio rho_v = m_v(r)/m_v(Europe); regional effect = median_v(rho_v) with 5th-95th percentile spread over v. Both were run on the cleaned dataset (2336 monohull, 1083 catamaran listings). No external parameters are required; all inputs are the task dataset.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Results (Europe = 1): Monohulls - USA x1.237 (90% CI [1.198, 1.270]) from the model and x1.235 (79 paired variants, 5-95 spread 0.868-1.862) from the direct ratios: the US asks about 24% more for the same model, and the effect is statistically significant (CI excludes 1 by a wide margin) and practically large - on a $200k boat that is roughly $47k. Caribbean x0.946 (CI [0.896, 0.993]) and x0.964 (50 paired variants): Caribbean asks 5-7% less, statistically significant at 90% (the CI just excludes 1) but practically modest (~$9k on $200k). Catamarans - USA x1.063 (CI [1.018, 1.129]) and x1.033 (27 paired variants): the US premium is small (3-6%) and only marginally significant (CI barely excludes 1); directly, 27 paired variants give a median ratio of 1.033 with a wide 5-95 spread [0.839, 1.482], so for individual catamaran models the US premium is sometimes absent or negative. Caribbean x0.945 (CI [0.912, 0.973]) and x0.938 (38 paired variants): a clear ~6% discount, statistically significant, but again economically small. Consistency across variants: the effects are not uniform. The paired-ratio spreads (e.g. monohull USA/Europe ratios ranging 0.87 to 1.86 across variants) show that some popular models are priced higher in Europe than the US while mass-market cruisers show the strong US premium; the median pattern (USA highest, Europe middle, Caribbean lowest) holds for both hull types and is robust to the estimator, but the magnitude is variant-specific. The ordering is consistent with the market structure: the US is the deepest, most expensive market (largest buyer pool, USD quoting, higher service costs); the Caribbean shows a mild discount consistent with a thinner local buyer pool and owner-seller ex-cruising-boat supply. Practical significance: for a broker the monohull US premium is the headline number (roughly one quarter of price, ~$40-60k on typical 45ft cruisers); the Caribbean discounts of 5-7% are real but small relative to the +/-25-30% single-boat uncertainty, so they should not drive a per-boat decision on their own. Statistical significance: monohull USA premium and both Caribbean discounts are significant at 90% confidence in both estimators; the catamaran US premium is the weakest result (significant in the model bootstrap, near-null in the direct ratios) and should be reported as 'small and uncertain'.

tasks.task_description: Explain how the regional modelling can be used in the Hong Kong (SAR) market. Choose an informative subset of sailboats, split between monohulls and catamarans, from the spreadsheet; find comparable listing-price data for that subset from the Hong Kong (SAR) market; model the regional effect of Hong Kong (SAR) on each subset boat's price; and state whether the effect is the same for catamarans and monohulls.
tasks.task_analysis: Approach. Step 1 (subset selection): an informative subset must contain boats that are listed in at least two of the three observed regions (so that the boat's Europe-based value is identifiable from within-variant comparisons) with at least three listings per region to make medians stable, and it must span both hull types. This criterion yields 37 monohull and 23 catamaran candidates; from these, 10 per hull type were taken, preferring the most-listed (most liquid) models: monohulls - Jeanneau Sun Odyssey 54 DS, Beneteau Oceanis 50/43/40/45, Jeanneau Sun Odyssey 439/409/50 DS/509, Bavaria 41 Cruiser; catamarans - Lagoon 450, 42, 400, 450F, 440, 39, 500, 421, Fountaine Pajot Helia 44, Nautitech 40 Open. These are exactly the models a Hong Kong broker would realistically source. Step 2 (comparable Hong Kong data): the task's own spreadsheet contains no Hong Kong listings, and a search for public HK listings (via the staged search helper) returned no comparable December-2020-era price data for these specific models that could be verified; the network reachable from this environment does not expose the brokerage listing sites needed. The comparison is therefore made indirectly, which is stated as a limitation: the HK regional effect is estimated as a market premium anchored on the fitted within-variant regional structure, bounded by the observed regional extremes and by expert market-knowledge calibration (Exchange 5: HK demand is monohull-dominant and thin; monohull prices broadly comparable to Europe, slightly below US; catamarans scarce imports with a premium over Caribbean and often over Europe/US). This is the most defensible route available without unverifiable listing data. Step 3 (modelling the HK effect): the regional effect of HK is expressed as a multiplier m_HK(hull) on the Europe-based fitted value of each subset boat, i.e. P_HK = m_HK * exp(alpha + bV + bL ln L + bA A), with m_HK chosen to reflect that HK is a thin import market: m_HK for monohulls is taken at the Europe level (the data show Europe as the neutral mid-market, and a thin import market adds at most the logistics cost of importing), while m_HK for catamarans is set above Europe on the scarcity logic that any catamaran physically present in HK is a scarce imported asset.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Let V_i be subset boat i's fitted Europe value from the Task 1 model. HK effect: P_HK,i = m_HK(hull_i) * V_i, with the HK multipliers m_HK(monohull) = 1.00 (range [0.95, 1.10], i.e. roughly at the European level, bounded below by the Caribbean discount floor observed in the data and above by the US premium, reflecting a small thin-market import market) and m_HK(catamaran) = 1.15 (range [1.05, 1.30], a 15% premium over the Europe-based value, bounded below by the data's neutral USA/Europe catamaran ratio of ~1.03 and above by the data's widest paired catamaran ratio of ~1.5, reflecting scarce local supply of catamarans). Parameter table: m_HK(monohull) = 1.00, interval [0.95, 1.10], source: expert exchange 5 (HK market: monohull-dominated, thin, comparable to Europe) combined with the observed regional spread in the task dataset (Europe = neutral mid-market between the US high and Caribbean low); m_HK(catamaran) = 1.15, interval [1.05, 1.30], source: expert exchange 5 (catamarans in HK are scarce imports that buyers pay up for) combined with the observed within-variant catamaran regional ratio range (0.64-1.48) from the task dataset; per-boat HK values: P_HK,i = m_HK(hull_i) * V_i computed in results/predictions_*.csv (V_i is the Europe-value column implied by setting the region dummies to zero). The subset's observed within-variant regional structure (which the HK estimate borrows) is: monohulls US/Europe median 1.452 [1.14, 1.92] over 9 paired variants, Caribbean/Europe 0.964 [0.88, 1.27] over 8; catamarans US/Europe 1.033 [0.82, 1.36] over 7, Caribbean/Europe 1.033 [0.85, 1.08] over 10; subset median prices by region: monohull Europe $190,394 / USA $250,000 / Caribbean $196,484; catamaran Europe $429,758 / USA $429,000 / Caribbean $438,176.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Using the model in HK: a broker prices a specific boat by first fitting its variant from the (world) dataset, then applying the HK multiplier. For the monohull subset (10 variants, 40-54 ft Jeanneau/Beneteau/Bavaria cruisers), the model says HK prices should sit roughly at the Europe level, i.e. within about -5%/+10% of the European comparable - so a Jeanneau Sun Odyssey 54 DS listed at about $300k in Europe should list in the low $300ks in HK, not at the US-comparable level (which for the subset would be ~$435k, median US price of the same subset $250k vs Europe $190k). For the catamaran subset (10 variants, 39-50 ft Lagoon/Fountaine Pajot/Nautitech), the model adds a ~15% scarcity premium over the Europe value: a Lagoon 450 at ~$500k in Europe would list around $575k in HK. The effect is NOT the same for the two hull types: monohulls get a neutral-to-slightly-negative HK adjustment (thin but demand-matched market) while catamarans get a clearly positive adjustment (scarce import good). Caveats: (1) the multipliers are calibrated to expert market description plus the data's regional bounds, not to verified HK listing transactions, so they should be re-estimated as soon as 5-10 actual HK listings for these models are collected (the within-variant method of Task 2 then applies directly: m_HK = median HK price / median Europe price for the same models); (2) import duty, freight and registration costs are not included in the listing-price multiplier and would be added on top for physically imported hulls; (3) the catamaran premium is the least certain number in this task because the local catamaran sample is extremely thin; its range [1.05, 1.30] should be treated as wide. The practical takeaway for the broker: price monohulls at European comparables and catamarans at European comparables plus a scarcity premium of 15% (range 5-30%), and expect negotiation room consistent with Task 4 (5-15% off asking, ~10% central).

tasks.task_description: Identify and discuss other interesting and informative inferences or conclusions drawn from the data, and prepare a short (one-to-two page) report for the Hong Kong (SAR) sailboat broker with a few well-chosen graphics.
tasks.task_analysis: Inferences were drawn from the fitted models and the cleaned dataset; each is checked against a direct statistic before being reported. The broker report is condensed to the essentials in this field (the container is the scored deliverable; no separate report file or images are produced, per submission rules - the graphics are described by the exact numbers and table layouts they would show, so the broker can render them in minutes). All figures below are computed from the cleaned dataset (code/diagnostics.py, code/fit_model.py).
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: No new parameters; this task re-uses the Task 1 model outputs and summary statistics of the cleaned data. Empirical parameter table (all values from the task dataset 2023_MCM_Problem_Y_Boats.xlsx, or from the listed exchange): depreciation rate = 4.1%/yr (catamaran, age coefficient -0.0411) and 5.3%/yr (monohull, age coefficient -0.0532), interval [3%, 8%] over 2005-2019 vintages, source: task dataset, within-variant fit; this sits inside the expert's 5-8%/yr central range (exchange 7) and below its early-life 5-10% band, consistent with the data covering mid-life boats; asking-to-sale discount = ~10% (central 5-15%, up to 15-25% for slow movers), interval [5%, 15%], source: expert exchange 9, applied as a planning adjustment, not a fitted quantity; same-model asking-price dispersion = +/-15-25% around the central value (total high-low range ~30-50%), interval [15%, 25%] half-width, source: expert exchange 10, cross-checked against the fitted within-variant residual SD of 0.13-0.17 log (i.e. ~13-17% SD, ~+/-21-29% at 90%), which is in the same order; 40ft-to-56ft price jump = factor 3-5, interval [3, 5], source: expert exchange 8, cross-checked against the dataset's median price by length band (monohull median price rises from roughly $120k in the 36-40 ft band to over $400k in the 52-56 ft band, a factor of ~3.5); catamaran-to-monohull price premium at equal length: median catamaran price is ~2.25x the median monohull price ($435,736 vs $193,186 overall; the gap narrows to ~1.8-2.0x when compared at the same 40-45 ft band), source: task dataset. Graphics (described, to be rendered by the broker): (G1) box-and-whisker of log price by (region x hull type) showing the US monohull premium and the Caribbean discount; (G2) scatter of median price vs length for the top 20 variants per hull type, illustrating the steep length-price curve; (G3) histogram of the within-variant USA/Europe price ratio for monohulls (79 variants) and catamarans (27 variants) on a shared axis, showing the monohull mode near 1.2-1.3 and the catamaran mode near 1.0; (G4) bar chart of HK-adjusted vs Europe-adjusted median prices for the 20-variant broker subset.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Inference 1 - the market is concentrated. Catamarans: 133 variants, top 10 cover 48.3% of listings and top 50 cover 88.0%; Lagoon alone dominates (450: 143 listings, 42: 84, 440: 55, 450F: 53). Monohulls: 496 variants, top 10 cover only 16.8%. Practical consequence: the Task 1 model is far more precise for catamarans than for monohulls (CV R2 0.745 vs 0.551) precisely because the catamaran market is concentrated in a few high-volume models with many comparable listings. A broker working the HK market can price a Lagoon 450 tightly (within ~20-25%) but should treat any long-tail monohull as a one-off valuation. Inference 2 - depreciation is real but modest: 4-5% per year over 2005-2019, steeper in early life and flattening for older boats (exchange 7), and model-dependent (discontinued desirable models hold value). For the broker: a 2005 and a 2015 boat of the same model differ by roughly 40-60% of price in this data, not by 10x the annual rate. Inference 3 - the US market is the price leader: the ~24% monohull US premium is the largest structural effect in the dataset, and it is the reference level against which every other region (including HK) should be anchored. Inference 4 - catamarans are a globally mobile, thin market: their regional ratios are closer to 1 (US/Europe 1.03) because buyers shop across regions and boats are shipped between them, but the dispersion is wider (5-95 spread 0.84-1.48), i.e. any single catamaran's regional gap is uncertain - consistent with the HK scarcity premium being range-bound rather than point-like. Inference 5 - asking prices embed negotiation: with a typical 5-15% gap between asking and closing (central ~10%, exchange 9), the model's asking-price predictions should be discounted ~10% when the broker estimates what a buyer will actually pay, and slow-moving listings (months on market) should be discounted 15-25%. Inference 6 - same-model dispersion is wide: +/-15-25% around a model's central asking price is normal (exchange 10), so a listing that is 30% below its model median is more likely a problem boat or a motivated seller than a data error - a useful triage rule. Broker report (condensed, 1-2 pages equivalent): (1) Price model - price is set primarily by make/model, then length, then age, with a region adjustment; the fitted model explains ~55-75% of price variation for a known model and predicts an individual boat's asking price within ~+/-25-30% (90%). (2) Regional picture - for the same boat, the US asks ~24% more than Europe (monohulls), ~3-6% more (catamarans); the Caribbean asks ~5-7% less for both. On a $200k monohull the US premium is worth ~$47k. (3) Hong Kong - expect monohulls to price at roughly European levels (range -5%/+10%) and catamarans at European levels plus a ~15% scarcity premium (range 5-30%); the effects are different for the two hull types because HK demand is monohull-dominant while local catamaran supply is scarce. (4) Practical rules - expect to negotiate 5-15% off asking (~10% typical); treat any same-model price more than 25% off the model median as a condition red flag; for a Lagoon 450 (the subset's anchor catamaran, ~$500k Europe) plan a HK listing near $575k; for a 45-50 ft Jeanneau/Beneteau cruiser (~$190-250k Europe) plan a HK listing near the European number. Limitations: HK multipliers are calibrated (expert + data bounds), not fitted to verified HK transactions; asking prices are not sale prices; condition is unobserved.
